title: Giving Willow Bend Creek More Room
description: Mixed Reading transfer practice on an evidence-based floodplain pilot.
subject: rla
author: Chee Skool
reviewNotes: Reviewed for transfer coverage, one-best-answer logic, qualified evidence, and GED-style reading targets.

questions.prompt: Why was the downstream peak near Cedar Avenue probably lower during the pilot storm, even though the rainfall total was similar to the earlier storm?

options.text: The new grasses absorbed nearly all of the storm water before it reached the creek.
options.whyWrong: The passage says the field temporarily held and slowed water; it does not say vegetation absorbed nearly all of it.

options.text: Some water spread into the upstream floodplain and returned to the channel later, reducing how much reached the bridge at the same moment.
The city widened the opening under the Cedar Avenue bridge during the pilot.
The second storm fell more slowly over several days, so the creek never received a sudden inflow.
options.whyWrong: The passage says the storms had similar totals but different weather patterns; it does not say the pilot storm lasted several days or lacked intense flow.

explanation.whyCorrect: The passage links temporary upstream storage with a lower peak near the bridge: water was spread out over time instead of arriving all at once.
explanation.quickTip: For an implied-cause question, combine the mechanism described earlier with the later result.
explanation.evidenceRef: The field could hold water that otherwise would arrive at the bridge all at once; during the test, water spread into the field for about four hours.

questions.prompt: What does the word “bottleneck” suggest about the bridge area in paragraph 6?

options.text: It is the safest place for storm water to remain after a flood.
options.whyWrong: The bridge area is described as a restriction, not a storage area.

options.text: It is a location where wildlife is unusually concentrated.
options.whyWrong: Wildlife observations concern the restored field, not the bridge.

options.text: It is a place where the creek becomes cleaner because water moves more slowly.
options.whyWrong: Water quality is not the point of the comparison.

options.text: It is a constricted point where more water can arrive than can pass through efficiently.

explanation.whyCorrect: “Bottleneck” suggests a narrow restriction that limits flow, matching the description of water reaching the bridge faster than its opening could carry it.
explanation.quickTip: Use the surrounding mechanism to identify the association a figurative word carries.
explanation.evidenceRef: Water rushed toward a low bridge ... faster than the opening beneath the bridge could carry it.

questions.prompt: Which word best describes the author’s tone toward the floodplain pilot?

options.text: Cautiously optimistic
Dismissive
options.whyWrong: The author treats the pilot as meaningful and worth continued study, not as unimportant.

options.text: Alarmed
options.whyWrong: Flooding is a serious topic, but the author’s treatment of the pilot is measured rather than fearful.

options.text: Triumphant
options.whyWrong: The passage repeatedly notes limits and does not claim the pilot solved flooding.

explanation.whyCorrect: The passage calls the results encouraging and describes possible benefits while repeatedly qualifying what the pilot has and has not proved.
explanation.quickTip: Tone should reflect the whole passage, especially both positive language and qualifications.
explanation.evidenceRef: The pilot has not eliminated flooding ... What it has provided is a test of a different principle.

questions.prompt: How does the organization of the passage help develop the author’s main idea?

options.text: It lists several flood-control methods from cheapest to most expensive so readers can choose one.
options.whyWrong: The passage follows one pilot project rather than ranking several methods by cost.

options.text: It presents residents’ objections after the final results so those objections appear unreasonable.
options.whyWrong: Residents’ concerns appear before the pilot results and are treated as legitimate questions.

options.text: It moves from the old flooding problem to the pilot design, then to results and limitations, showing why the new approach is promising but still being evaluated.
It alternates between two engineers with opposing views to show that experts cannot agree.
options.whyWrong: The passage does not alternate between opposing engineers.

explanation.whyCorrect: The sequence lets readers see the problem, understand the intervention, examine evidence, and then see why the conclusion remains qualified.
explanation.quickTip: A structure-effect answer should explain what the organization allows the author to demonstrate, not merely summarize sections.
explanation.evidenceRef: The passage progresses from repeated flooding, to the pilot, to its first test, limitations, and the decision to monitor another season.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the author’s point of view about restoring floodplains as a flood-control strategy?

options.text: Restored floodplains should replace conventional drainage systems in every city.
options.whyWrong: The author explicitly says the design may not work on every stream.

options.text: They are a promising strategy that should be judged with continued monitoring and local evidence.
They are mainly valuable because they attract wildlife, while flood reduction is secondary.
options.whyWrong: Habitat is presented as an unexpected benefit, not the primary purpose.

options.text: They are too uncertain to justify testing until engineers can isolate every variable.
options.whyWrong: The passage treats the pilot itself as a useful way to gather evidence despite uncertainty.

explanation.whyCorrect: The author presents the strategy as worth testing and potentially useful while emphasizing limits, confounding factors, and the need for more data.
explanation.quickTip: Author point of view often appears in the balance between what the text endorses and what it refuses to overclaim.
explanation.evidenceRef: Mason City plans to collect data through another wet season ... the pilot has not proved that the same design would work on every stream.

curriculum.learningObjective: Transfer inference, connotation, tone, structure, and point-of-view reasoning to an original informational passage.
